subject: Business
title: Open Innovation: Ideas from Outside
description: A fast breakdown of Open Innovation: Ideas from Outside for builders.

hook.text: Procter & Gamble's CEO admitted: 'Most innovation doesn't come from our own labs anymore.'

buildup.text: Open innovation means using external ideas, partnerships, and technologies alongside internal R&D.

discovery.text: P&G's Connect + Develop program sources half its innovations externally. It cut R&D costs significantly.

twist.text: The challenge: internal teams resist external ideas. 'Not invented here' syndrome kills promising imports.

climax.text: Linux, Wikipedia, and Android all prove that open collaboration can outperform closed R&D.

punchline.text: The smartest people don't all work for you. Invite them in.

quiz.question: What is the 'not invented here' syndrome?
options: Internal resistance to ideas that come from outside the organization
A legal issue with importing foreign products
A problem with patent filing across countries

details.summary: Open innovation recognizes that valuable ideas can originate outside an organization as well as inside. Coined by Henry Chesbrough, it encourages companies to use external ideas, technologies, and talent alongside internal R&D to accelerate innovation and reduce development costs.
details.whyItMatters: No company has a monopoly on good ideas. Open innovation taps the global talent pool through partnerships, licensing, crowdsourcing, and acquisitions. Companies that innovate only internally miss opportunities while bearing all R&D costs alone.
takeaways: Valuable innovation can come from outside an organization's boundaries
Inbound open innovation adopts external ideas for internal products
Outbound open innovation licenses internal ideas for external use

faq.question: What are practical examples of open innovation?
faq.answer: Procter & Gamble's Connect+Develop sources over 50% of innovations externally. NASA's open challenges on crowdsourcing platforms. Pharmaceutical companies licensing drug candidates from universities. Tech companies acquiring startups for technology. LEGO crowdsourcing product designs from fans.

faq.question: What are the risks of open innovation?
faq.answer: Intellectual property leakage when sharing with external partners. Coordination costs of managing multiple external relationships. Quality control challenges with externally sourced ideas. Difficulty integrating external innovations with internal systems. Cultural resistance from internal R&D teams.
